newsitem.title: UK: Heating oil buyers keep crude prices on the boil.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil buyers keep crude prices on the boil.

text.p: An increasingly desperate scramble to recharge depleted winter heating oil stocks in Europe and the United States on Monday took oil prices to their highest level since the Gulf War of 1991.
London November futures for world benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil closed at $24.45 a barrel, a 64 cent gain on the day after a breathless rally in the last few minutes of trade on Monday.
This was the highest price for near-month crude since a high of $31.20 a barrel was achieved in January 1991, when the U.S.-led alliance began its offensive against Iraqi occupying forces in Kuwait.
Brokers said there was no news behind Monday's late rally and heating oil remained the driving force behind higher crude oil prices.

The first chill of winter weather over the weekend in the U.S. northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, exacerbated worries about inventories of heating oil, which are already running about one third down on last year.
Meteorologist Weather Services Corp said temperatures in the U.S. northeast were as much as seven degrees Celsius (14 Fahrenheit) below normal at the weekend.
Even higher heating oil prices than in the United States are set to draw a fleet of cargoes across the Atlantic this month.
Worried refinery buyers, concerned that an early cold snap could eat into their depleted stocks, hedged against price rises on futures exchanges and speculators bet on further price gains.
"It's just more of the same," said one London futures broker of the price rises. "People buying heating oil."
Dealers said the only risk to oil prices appeared to be a wholesale turnaround in market sentiment.
"The only thing bearish in the markets is that it's full of bulls," said one trader.
Analysts said higher than expected demand for oil this year was also keeping crude oil prices near five-year highs despite rising world supplies.
"We think demand is at least 200,000 barrels a day higher (than previously expected) for this year assuming just a normal winter," said oil analyst Mehdi Varzi at bankers Kleinwort Benson.

On the supply side, although most OPEC members continue to to flout self-imposed quotas, the handful of Middle East OPEC members with extra capacity -- Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and to a lesser extent Kuwait -- have so far not been enticed into raising output significantly.

OPEC wellhead crude output in September was just about unchanged at 25.86 million barrels per day (bpd) from a revised 25.87 million in August, a Reuter survey of OPEC, industry officials and analysts found.
Slightly lower production from OPEC's biggest supplier Saudi Arabia along with Nigeria balanced higher volumes from Qatar, Iran and Indonesia, the survey found.
